newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Kohl govt mulls ways to plug deficit gap.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kohl govt mulls ways to plug deficit gap.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government searched on Thursday for ways to plug gaping holes in the 1997 and 1998 budgets, with coalition financial experts examining a wide array of proposals.

Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) suggested introducing a tax on life insurance in 1998 that would raise 3.5 billion marks ($2 billion), coalition sources said. But the centrist Free Democrats (FDP) denied a report they had agreed to the proposal.

The coalition partners, struggling to close a total gap of some 50 billion marks for 1997 and 1998 and help Germany qualify for Europe's single currency, have been at odds for weeks on the budget. The FDP has adamantly opposed tax increases that Finance Minister Theo Waigel and conservatives say may be unavoidable.
"I am confident that the negotiations will lead to a good result," said FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt. He declined to provide details but said there were a wide range of possibilities being discussed.

Coalition sources said there was still considerable discord over plans to close corporate tax loopholes that currently enable companies to carry forward losses into more profitable years and offset those against taxes.

But coalition partners were in agreement on the plan to partially plug the deficits by selling government holdings. They hope to reap 25 billion marks over two years by selling Deutsche Telekom shares.
The financial experts were also studying new ideas on budget cutting that could save as much as four billion marks and reduce spending on job creation schemes.

In Munich, the Ifo economic institute said Germany's 1997 budget deficit would exceed the Maastricht Treaty ceiling but it would not prevent Germany from qualifying for economic and monetary union (EMU).
Ifo said Germany's overall state budget deficit would be just under 120 billion marks ($69 billion), or 3.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), this year.
The Maastricht Treaty states a three-percent deficit to GDP ratio ceiling for countries wishing to join the single currency, scheduled to start in January 1999.
A leading member of Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) called on Kohl to link a parliamentary vote on his 1998 budget in July to a confidence motion, a newspaper said.
If Kohl lost such a confidence vote, the way could be opened for general elections now likely to be held in September 1998 to be brought forward a year.

"If the Chancellor can no longer manage his business properly then, he should have the courage to go before the Bundestag (lower house) and ask the confidence question," Peter Struck, SPD parliamentary whip told the Bildwoche weekly.

Struck said the FDP had to put itself on the line. Either the party would betray its tax-cutting principles and follow the CDU/Christian Social Union into election defeat or vote against the Chancellor and show its commitment to lower taxes, he said. ($ = 1.731 German Marks)
